title: Quantum Pessiland
authors: Boyang Chen, Tomoyuki Morimae, Takashi Yamakawa
abstract: Pessiland is a world where NP is hard on average but one-way functions (OWFs) do not exist [Impagliazzo 1995]. Because almost all classical cryptographic primitives imply OWFs [Impagliazzo and Luby 1989], there is almost no classical cryptography in Pessiland. On the other hand, quantum cryptography can exist even when OWFs do not [Kretschmer 2021; Morimae and Yamakawa 2022; Ananth, Qian and Yuen 2022]. Is there a quantum analogue of Pessiland where NP is hard on average but even quantum cryptography does not exist? In this paper, we show that such a miserable world, Quantum Pessiland, exists: there is a quantum oracle relative to which $UP\cap coUP$ is hard on average against quantum polynomial-time algorithms with quantum advice, yet auxiliary-input EFI pairs do not exist. We also show that there is a classical oracle relative to which $UP\cap coUP$ is hard on average against quantum polynomial-time algorithms with quantum advice, yet classically-secure auxiliary-input one-way puzzles (OWPuzzs) do not exist. Almost all quantum cryptographic primitives imply EFI pairs or OWPuzzs, and therefore these results mean that there is almost no quantum cryptography relative to these oracles. We further show that relative to the classical oracle, SampBQP = SampBPP, and therefore there is no sampling-based quantum advantage in Quantum Pessiland. Finally, because our average-case hardness of $UP\cap coUP$ implies $P^{\#P}\not\subseteq i.o.BQP/qpoly$, our result also implies that a non-relativizing proof technique is necessary to construct OWPuzzs solely from $P^{\#P}\not\subseteq i.o.BQP/qpoly$, which gives a partial negative answer to the open problem of [Khurana and Tomer 2025].
summary: This paper explores 'Quantum Pessiland,' a theoretical model where computational hardness exists, but quantum cryptography fails. By constructing specific oracles, the authors prove that the non-existence of quantum primitives like EFI pairs is implied by average-case hardness assumptions. This work provides deep insights into the necessary computational assumptions required for quantum cryptography to function.
main_problem: The paper investigates the existence of 'Quantum Pessiland,' a theoretical setting where computational hardness (NP hard on average) holds, but no quantum cryptographic primitives (like OWFs or EFI pairs) can exist.
main_result: The authors prove the existence of such a world relative to specific oracles, demonstrating that almost no quantum cryptography exists under these conditions, and further showing no sampling-based quantum advantage.
method: The proof relies on constructing specific quantum and classical oracles and using advanced techniques involving the Patching Lemma to show that the average-case hardness of $	ext{UP} \cap 	ext{coUP}$ implies the non-existence of necessary cryptographic primitives.
model_or_system: The model is purely theoretical, based on quantum complexity theory, utilizing quantum oracles, quantum advice, and cryptographic primitives like auxiliary-input EFI pairs and OWPuzzs.
key_observables: Statistical distance (SD) between quantum distributions, average-case hardness of $	ext{UP} \cap 	ext{coUP}$, and the existence/non-existence of specific quantum primitives.
important_parameters: The analysis involves parameters related to the required accuracy of simulations, such as $r(n)$ and the number of repetitions $R$.
main_assumptions: The results are conditional on the existence of specific oracles and rely on advanced techniques like the exponential moment to overcome the limitations of auxiliary inputs.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon classical Pessiland concepts, first establishing results relative to a classical oracle (Theorem 1.1), then extending to a quantum oracle (Theorem 1.2), and finally analyzing implications for sampling-based advantage and open problems in complexity theory.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, the work pushes the boundaries of quantum complexity theory by establishing precise boundaries on what quantum computation can achieve cryptographically, which is fundamental to understanding quantum information limits.
